papers.title: How to Read a Paper
papers.abstract: Researchers spend a great deal of time reading research papers. However, this skill is rarely taught, leading to much wasted effort. This article outlines a practical and efficient three-pass method for reading research papers. I also describe how to use this method to do a literature survey.
papers.notes:
as a undergrad student (2026), i can clearly say that this was all i was looking for. 

Apr 26 2026, i suddenly googled as "how to read a paper" an this was what I faced with.

To conclude, this paper suggests a three-pass approach to read articles for more efficient way.

pass one -> quickly skim the headings, abstraction and conclusion. approx. 10-15min

pass two -> read more deeply, but do not interfere with proofs if it is a technical paper;mark relevant unread references for further reading. pay attention to figures. approx. 1hr

pass three -> basically re-implement the paper. you need to think as author and brainstorm about the complex structures and criticize the limitations. approx. 4-5 hr

papers.title: Topological turning points across the human lifespa
papers.abstract: Structural topology develops non-linearly across the lifespan and is strongly related to cognitive trajectories. We gathered diffusion imaging from datasets with a collective age range of zero to 90 years old (N = 4,216). We analyzed how 12 graph theory metrics of organization change with age and projected these data into manifold spaces using Uniform Manifold Projection and Approximation. With these manifolds, we identified four major topological turning points across the lifespan – around nine, 32, 66, and 83 years old. These ages defined five major epochs of topological development, each with distinctive age-related changes in topology. These lifespan epochs each have a distinct direction of topological development and specific changes in the organizational properties driving the age-topology relationship. This study underscores the complex, non-linear nature of human development, with unique phases of topological maturation, which can only be illuminated with a multivariate, lifespan, population-level perspective.
papers.notes:
"With these manifolds, we identified four major topological turning points across the lifespan – around nine, 32, 66, and 83 years old"

these 4 major topology changes tell us that our brain development persists in connecting new synapses until the age of 32. From 32 to 66, it reaches a plateau. i keep thinking about this article's philosophical perspective on aging. the study shows that the government classifies people under 18 as children, but this is not the case. between the ages of 9 and 32, an 18-year-old and a 28-year-old exhibit an approximately similar brain structure.

to be honest, i am a little bit relieved. this is because, i do not feel "smart" or "sharp-minded" enough these days.

papers.title: Variational quantum algorithms
papers.abstract:
VQAs have already been considered for a plethora of
applications (see Figure 3), covering essentially all of the applications that researchers had envisioned for quantum computers. Although they may be the key to obtaining near-term quantum advantage, VQAs still face important challenges, including their trainability, accuracy,and efficiency.In this Review, we discuss the exciting prospects for VQAs, and we highlight the challenges that must be overcome to obtain the ultimate goal of quantum advantage.
papers.notes: this paper essentially reviews and consolidates a comprehensive collection of literature on variational quantum algorithms (vqas) into a single framework. the core architecture of a vqa consists of three key components: an ansatz, which is a parameterized quantum circuit used to represent trainable parameters; a cost function that maps quantum states to a high-dimensional landscape that needs to be optimized; and classical optimizers that use gradients to minimize this cost function. however, a critical challenge in training vqas is the phenomenon of barren plateaus, which occurs when gradients vanish and become exponentially close to zero, rendering the optimization landscape flat and making the circuit untrainable.

papers.title: Competitive Programmer's Handbook
papers.abstract:
The purpose of this book is to give you a thorough introduction to competitive
programming. It is assumed that you already know the basics of programming,
but no previous background in competitive programming is needed.
The book is especially intended for students who want to learn algorithms
and possibly participate in the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) or in
the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC). Of course, the book is
also suitable for anybody else interested in competitive programming.
It takes a long time to become a good competitive programmer, but it is also
an opportunity to learn a lot. You can be sure that you will get a good general
understanding of algorithms if you spend time reading the book, solving problems
and taking part in contests.
papers.notes: This resource is basically Holy Bible for competitive programming. It includes every intuition for every problem. Providing a detailed insights about defining a problem with their constraints/rules. Every CS student needs to read this.

papers.title: AUTO-AVSR: AUDIO-VISUAL SPEECH RECOGNITION WITH AUTOMATIC LABELS
papers.abstract:
Audio-visual speech recognition has received a lot of attention due
to its robustness against acoustic noise. Recently, the performance of
automatic, visual, and audio-visual speech recognition (ASR, VSR,
and AV-ASR, respectively) has been substantially improved, mainly
due to the use of larger models and training sets. However, accu-
rate labelling of datasets is time-consuming and expensive. Hence,
in this work, we investigate the use of automatically-generated tran-
scriptions of unlabelled datasets to increase the training set size. For
this purpose, we use publicly-available pre-trained ASR models to
automatically transcribe unlabelled datasets such as AVSpeech and
VoxCeleb2. Then, we train ASR, VSR and AV-ASR models on
the augmented training set, which consists of the LRS2 and LRS3
datasets as well as the additional automatically-transcribed data. We
demonstrate that increasing the size of the training set, a recent trend
in the literature, leads to reduced WER despite using noisy tran-
scriptions. The proposed model achieves new state-of-the-art per-
formance on AV-ASR on LRS2 and LRS3. In particular, it achieves
a WER of 0.9 % on LRS3, a relative improvement of 30 % over the
current state-of-the-art approach, and outperforms methods that have
been trained on non-publicly available datasets with 26 times more
training data.
papers.notes: after a decade of lipnet's dominance in controlled settings, auto-avsr completely revolutionized the audio-visual speech recognition landscape by shattering the manual labeling bottleneck; by leveraging an automated pipeline to train on thousands of hours of raw, unlabelled videos using a powerful conformer architecture, it shifted the field from brittle, lab-based lip-reading to a robust, scalable multimodal system that delivers unprecedented word error rates in chaotic, real-world conditions.

papers.title: WaveNet: A Generative Model for Raw Audio
papers.authors: Aaron van den Oord, Sander Dieleman, Heiga Zen, Karen Simonyan, Oriol Vinyals, Alex Graves, Nal Kalchbrenner, Andrew Senior, Koray Kavukcuoglu
papers.abstract: This paper introduces WaveNet, a deep neural network for generating raw audio waveforms. The model is fully probabilistic and autoregressive, with the predictive distribution for each audio sample conditioned on all previous ones; nonetheless we show that it can be efficiently trained on data with tens of thousands of samples per second of audio. When applied to text-to-speech, it yields state-of-the-art performance, with human listeners rating it as significantly more natural sounding than the best parametric and concatenative systems for both English and Mandarin. A single WaveNet can capture the characteristics of many different speakers with equal fidelity, and can switch between them by conditioning on the speaker identity. When trained to model music, we find that it generates novel and often highly realistic musical fragments. We also show that it can be employed as a discriminative model, returning promising results for phoneme recognition.
papers.notes: I personally really liked this paper imlementing this. The flattening layer seperation is really intuitive. 10/10. Thank you DeepMind

posts.title: my bachelor's thesis, explained without the scary words
posts.summary: what exponential concentration in quantum kernels is, plus a deliberately short look at my thesis while the paper is under review.
posts.body:
my bachelor's thesis is done, and the paper that came out of it is under review at Quantum Machine Intelligence. it's not public yet, so this post stays on the surface on purpose. the details can wait until it's out.

my advisor is Assoc. Prof. Ammar Daskin, and my co-author is Latif Akgün.

## the problem, without the scary words

a kernel is just a similarity score. you take two data points, you ask "how alike are these?", and you get a number. a model like an SVM learns everything from a big table of those numbers.

in a quantum kernel, each data point becomes a quantum state, and with n qubits that state lives in a space with 2ⁿ dimensions. that is a huge room. and in a huge room, two random-ish directions are almost always close to perpendicular. so the similarity between any two different points is almost zero.

now the table has 1 on the diagonal (everything is similar to itself) and nearly the same tiny number everywhere else. the model looks at it and sees no structure. every point is a stranger to every other point. people call this **exponential concentration**: the values collapse towards one number, exponentially fast as you add qubits.

and you only get a finite number of measurements. once the differences between points are smaller than the noise, there is nothing left to learn. more qubits, more power, less signal. funny.

## what we did, the short version

the thesis asks a simple question: does the kernel really need all of its parts? we keep the parts that carry the structure and leave the rest out, and we do it without ever looking at the labels, so nothing secretly peeks at the answers.

that's all i'll say for now. how we pick the parts, and how well it works, is for the paper.

## what the year looked like

my first proposal didn't survive the summer. it turned out to be something that already existed under another name. annoying, but i'd rather find that out in august than in a review. a lot of the thesis after that was learning one small piece at a time and writing it down.

finishing is quieter than i expected, mostly a pdf. but i can now explain the problem with a room full of perpendicular arrows, which i could not do a year ago. i'll take that. once the paper is out, i'll come back and write the real version of this post.

posts.title: what a turkish lipreading model taught me about shrinking problems
posts.summary: notes from a closed lipreading project, why open-vocabulary lipreading is brutal, and why picking a smaller problem got me further than adding more data.
posts.body:
i just closed my lipreading project. it started in March as Microsoft-mentored research on AI for accessibility: a silent communication tool for people with speech impairments, built by my team and me. the idea is simple. you mouth a word, the computer reads your lips, and the word shows up. no voice needed.

the working prototype is still online ([try it here](https://uuu4--lipreading-prototip-web.us-east.modal.run)), and i'm leaving it up. here is what i actually learned, mostly the hard way.

## open vocabulary is brutal

our first real model was supposed to read free sentences in Turkish. we took a model pretrained on English lipreading and fine-tuned it on Turkish videos. the result was a word error rate of 87.1%. if you are not used to that number: it means the model gets roughly 9 words out of 10 wrong.

before the run i had guessed 55 to 75% error, then bumped it to 65 to 80%. i was off by a lot, and that was not the only prediction i got wrong that month. my pattern was always the same: i noticed one true thing and then inflated it into a big promise.

why is it so hard? because lips are a bad channel. many different sounds look identical from outside. try saying "bir", "ben", "bin" and "biz" in front of a mirror. in our data about a quarter of words had a lookalike. it gets worse in Turkish, where words are built by sticking endings onto a root. "olduğu" and "olduğunu" share the whole beginning, and the part that tells them apart is a tiny quick movement at the very end. the model confused exactly those pairs, again and again. that was weirdly satisfying, in a sad way: its mistakes were not random, they were the same ones a human would make.

## the thing that surprised me

for months i was chasing more data. more hours, more speakers. then one training run made me realise that the amount of data was not what was blocking us.

so i asked a different question. what does a person who cannot speak actually need? not Turkish literature. they need to say "water", "it hurts", "toilet". a small, fixed list.

so we switched to a **closed vocabulary**: the model only chooses from a list of words, instead of spelling out anything. same frozen model, with just a tiny classifier on top. it is a different question, not a different brain. on a list of 20 distinct words it reached 67%, while the same model on free speech was getting maybe one word in eight right. nothing about the model changed. the problem got smaller.

this is the lesson i will keep. before you make the model stronger, ask if you are solving a problem that is too big. a lot of the "intelligence" of the final prototype is just the person who picks the word list.

two details helped. long words are much easier than short ones, because there is more mouth movement to see. and whole phrases beat single words by a huge margin, again for the same reason.

## what i'd do differently

- record the real vocabulary earlier. our training videos were not people saying "water" on purpose. the data i needed was small and specific, and i collected the wrong kind first.
- decide on the closed vocabulary much earlier, instead of after months of collecting data.
- measure with more care. i once reported a nice improvement from 150 test examples. with 500 it shrank to about half. small samples lie.
- test on people who are not me as soon as possible. i only measured the final prototype on myself, which is a real limit, and i'd rather say it out loud.

the project is closed now. it is not a product and i won't pretend it is. but it works for a small word list, and it taught me to shrink the problem before scaling the model.

posts.title: what happens if you give eyes to a language model?
posts.summary: how google's paligemma 2 turns an image into words, and a small turkish ocr test of its claim that resolution matters more than size for reading text.
posts.body: *Reading Google's PaliGemma 2 paper, and testing it on Turkish text* I showed the same cigarette box to two versions of the same AI model. One read the warning. The other read half of it, then added a sentence that is not on the pack: "Buzdolabında saklayın", which means "store in the fridge". That odd mistake is where this post starts. PaliGemma 2 is Google's open model that looks at an image and answers in text, and its paper makes a claim I wanted to test on Turkish. ## Introduction PaliGemma 2 changes one thing from the first PaliGemma: the language model becomes Gemma 2, in three sizes (3B, 10B, 28B) and three input resolutions (224, 448 and 896 pixels), with the same SigLIP-So400m vision encoder. It also gained new abilities such as text recognition. ## The Eye: SigLIP The first part of the architecture is SigLIP, a contrastive vision encoder. It takes an image and turns it into a series of embeddings. So what does "contrastive" mean? ![PaliGemma architecture: SigLIP vision encoder, linear projection and Gemma decoder](assets/posts/paligemma2/01-architecture.jpg) ![Contrastive pre-training: image and text encoders, N by N score matrix](assets/posts/paligemma2/02-contrastive.jpg) We have a batch of N (image, caption) pairs. The images pass through the image encoder, the captions through the text encoder, and the dot product of every image vector with every text vector gives an N×N score matrix: ``` "cat" "car" "sea" img_cat [ 5 1 0 ] img_car [ 0 4 1 ] img_sea [ 1 0 3 ] ``` Training pushes the diagonal up and everything else down. That is why it is called "contrastive": it learns by comparing the correct pair against the wrong ones, and those negatives keep the model from collapsing. The loss is a softmax over each row followed by cross entropy; SigLIP replaces the softmax with a sigmoid, so every pair becomes its own yes/no question, which is easier to parallelize and allows a bigger batch. It needs billions of (image, caption) pairs, but they are crawled from the internet with their descriptions, so no manual labeling is needed. The vision transformer SigLIP is built on: ![Image patches flattened into embeddings with positional encoding added](assets/posts/paligemma2/03-patch-embeddings.jpg) The difference from a normal transformer is that the input is a set of pixel groups (patches) instead of text. Each patch is flattened into a single vector, merging neighbouring elements into one, an idea we know from WaveNet. Flattening loses positional information, so the embeddings pass through a learned positional encoding layer. ![Vision transformer turning patch embeddings into contextualized embeddings](assets/posts/paligemma2/04-vit-encoder.jpg) What SigLIP can do is answer "which of these texts matches this image?" with a score. When we ask "what does the sign say?", we hit its limits. For that we need a language model. ## The Language Model and Putting It Together Now we can move on to the actual PaliGemma architecture: ![Full PaliGemma pipeline, image tokens placed in front of the prompt](assets/posts/paligemma2/05-paligemma.jpg) The text is turned into numbers with Google's SentencePiece tokenizer, concatenated with the image tokens and fed to the language model. In one sentence: SigLIP turns the image into "words" that Gemma can read, and put in front of the prompt without touching Gemma's architecture, they become its "eyes". PaliGemma does many different jobs not by changing the code but by changing the prompt. ![Token sequence: image tokens and question as prefix, answer as suffix](assets/posts/paligemma2/06-sequence.png) For Gemma the image is nothing but a few words. The user's prompt is appended after them, and then Gemma generates the output. ## How an Image Becomes Tokens If you want to try this yourself, here is the interactive guide we made: [How PaliGemma Reads](https://claude.ai/artifact/XytgheoWTwkAJqxgBQdTDw) ![Interactive guide: a street sign cut into 14 by 14 pixel patches](assets/posts/paligemma2/07-patches.png) The image is resized to 224x224 pixels and cut into 14x14 pixel patches, each of which becomes one image "word": 224 / 14 = 16 patches per side, so 16x16 = 256 image words. At 448 it is 32x32 = 1024 tokens, at 896 it is 64x64 = 4096. This may be why small text is read better at 448: the text is spread across more patches. A linear layer turns each patch (14x14x3 = 588 numbers) into a vector of 1152 numbers and a position embedding is added. Over 27 unmasked transformer layers every patch looks at all the others. The 1152-dimensional vectors are then projected to Gemma's 2304 dimensions, so they match the prompt's tokens and can be concatenated with them. The prompt is split with the SentencePiece tokenizer, and the 256 `` placeholders in front of it are replaced by the image tokens right before Gemma. ## Attention Mask and Generation The most crucial detail in this architecture is the attention mask we use. In the GPT series (mostly decoder-only), every word sees only the words before it, like a `torch.tril` mask. Here is the problem: image tokens cannot see the question, because the question comes after them. ![GPT-style causal attention mask](assets/posts/paligemma2/08-mask-causal.png) *A GPT-style mask: every token sees only the ones before it.* In a vision transformer (vision encoder), on the other hand, everyone sees everyone. That is good for reading, but it cannot be used to generate an answer, because the future can be seen. ![Vision transformer full attention mask](assets/posts/paligemma2/09-mask-full.png) *A vision transformer: every token sees every other token.* ![PaliGemma prefix-LM attention mask](assets/posts/paligemma2/10-mask-prefix.png) *PaliGemma combines the two: the image and question are fully visible, the answer is written step by step.* The prefix (image + prompt) is fully open, meaning every token sees every token. The answer words see the whole prefix plus the answer words before them. First look at the whole, then write the answer word by word with the same loop as in any GPT: predict, append, repeat until EOS. ## Findings of the Paper ![PaliGemma 2 paper, Figure 4: transfer performance by model size and resolution](assets/posts/paligemma2/11-scaling.jpg) The colors in the plot group tasks by what they are sensitive to: yellow tasks (text-heavy ones such as DocVQA, TextVQA, ST-VQA, TextCaps, ChartQA) barely improve with model size, but the 448 line is much higher, so they are sensitive to resolution. Blue ones (AI2D, MaRVL, NLVR2, ScienceQA) improve with model size. The paper gives a reason: the images in these text-heavy benchmarks "often have a native resolution significantly larger than 224px²" (Section 4.1), so a small input throws away detail that a larger one keeps. What the paper does not say is whether that still holds when the text is not English. ## The Gap The paper evaluates multilinguality with four benchmarks (COCO-35L, XM3600, xGQA, MaRVL), half captioning and half question answering and reasoning, yet the text reading (OCR) tasks, shown as one of the model's strongest sides, are measured in English. So the effect of resolution on multilingual OCR cannot be read from the paper. We ran a Turkish OCR benchmark ourselves. ## Experiment: Turkish OCR, 224 vs 448 **Setup:** `paligemma2-3b-mix-224` and `-448` on a Colab T4 (bf16, greedy, `max_new_tokens=100`), 11 photos I took myself (7 receipts, 3 cigarette boxes, 1 sign) and five prompts: `ocr`, and `answer en` and `answer tr`, each with an English and a Turkish question, so the language code and the language of the question can be told apart. I ran all 110 outputs in three separate Colab sessions. Code, raw outputs and a script that rebuilds the tables: https://github.com/uuu4/paligemma-tr-benchmark **Measurement:** the word match is the share of the first words of the text on each photo (receipt: the business name; box and sign: the start of the warning) found exactly in the output, Turkish characters included. Invented words are output words that are not on the photo and not a one-letter slip of one that is (I wrote down each photo's full text to count them). **Table 1: average word match (%), 224 / 448.** Last session; in brackets, the range over the three sessions where they differed. | Group | `ocr` | `answer en`, English question | `answer tr`, English question | `answer tr`, Turkish question | `answer en`, Turkish question | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Boxes + sign (4) | 44 / 86 | 44 / 86 | 44 / 86 | 35 / 81 | 20 / 56 | | Receipt headers (7) | 84 (70-84) / 78 | 80 / 78 | 80 (77-80) / 71 | 29 / 39 (39-61) | 21 / 39 | **Table 2: per photo, `ocr`** (last session) | Photo | Letter, in patches (224 / 448) | `ocr` 224 | `ocr` 448 | Invented words (224 / 448) | |---|---|---|---|---| | kutu_01 | 0.25 / 0.50 | 40 | 100 | 13 / 1 | | kutu_02 | 0.25 / 0.50 | 60 | 100 | 2 / 2 | | kutu_03 | 0.25 / 0.50 | 57 | 86 | 11 / 5 | | tabela_01, small text | 0.32 / 0.63 | 20 | 60 | 7 / 0 | | fis_01 | 0.44 / 0.88 | 75 | 100 | 1 / 1 | | fis_02 | 0.44 / 0.88 | 100 | 100 | 2 / 0 | | fis_03 | 0.33 / 0.66 | 100 | 67 | 8 / 1 | | fis_04 | 0.44 / 0.88 | 75 | 100 | 1 / 0 | | fis_05 | 0.44 / 0.88 | 40 | 80 | 7 / 1 | | fis_06 | 0.78 / 1.56 | 100 | 0 | 7 / 5 | | fis_07 | 0.44 / 0.88 | 100 | 100 | 1 / 0 | *Letter heights are my estimates (receipts about 70 px, boxes 63, the sign's small text 80). Letter in patches = letter px x input size / photo height / 14. In one session fis_06 scored 0 at 224; all other rows were the same in all three.* **Small, dense text.** On the boxes and the sign, 448 reads far better (`ocr` 44% to 86%, identical in all three sessions), as in the paper's English tasks. **Receipt headers.** The gain disappears: 84% at 224 against 78% at 448 in the last session, which is inside the noise. Across the three sessions 224 scored 84, 70 and 84 and 448 gave 78 every time; one photo (fis_06) flipped between a correct read and a string of digits, worth 14 points. So "no gain on receipts" holds, but "448 is worse" does not. **Letter size.** Once a photo is squeezed to the square input, a receipt letter is about 0.4 of a 14-pixel patch at 224, and a box letter or the sign's small text 0.25 to 0.3. These smallest letters gained most from 448 (+42 points, against -6 to +8 on receipts). The sign shows it in one photo: its heading, 1.5 patches tall, is read at both sizes, while the small lines under it are invented at 224 and read almost correctly at 448. With 11 photos and guessed letter sizes, this is a hint, not a result. **Invented words.** The opening example was not a one-off. On the box and sign photos the 224 model invents 33 to 34 words per session against 4 to 8 for 448, and "Buzdolabında saklayın" appears on two of the three boxes in every session. The 448 model fails differently: it loops ("Üzerinde" three times, once a long string of zeros). On receipts 224 also invents more (13, 14 and 27 words against 8, 9 and 8), but that count moves a lot between sessions. **The Turkish question.** What breaks reading is the Turkish question, not the language code. With an English question the model reads the receipts under both codes (80% at 224; at 448, 78% and 71%). With a Turkish question it gives a short description such as 'a sign that says "sigara içilmez"': 29% at 224 in all three sessions, 39 to 61% at 448. **Limitations:** N=11; three boxes of one brand and one sign; the targets are only the first words; letter heights are estimates; the full texts behind the invented-word count are my own reading. Repeats inside one Colab session were identical, but across three sessions 28 to 46 outputs differed, so I give ranges. ## Conclusion To wrap up: the paper's most interesting finding is that text-heavy tasks care more about resolution than model size, but it measures them in English. In my Turkish test the boxes and the sign agree (`ocr` 44% at 224, 86% at 448 in all three sessions, and 224 invents four to eight times more words), the receipts show no gain beyond the noise, and it is the Turkish question, not the language code, that stops the model from reading. This is a hint, not proof. Next I would try the 10B `mix-448` checkpoint and more varied photos (the `mix` checkpoints exist only at 224 and 448). There is also a video version of this post on my YouTube channel, Ariadne: https://youtu.be/7kT2QCFOhzk Sources: the PaliGemma 2 paper (arXiv 2412.03555) and Umar Jamil's PaliGemma video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vAmKB7iPkWw). Thanks for reading!
